account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings, and algorithms checked the photos. Penn State also extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. The wider operation also used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. On 8 April 2021 The New York Times reported that PlantVillage scouts, government personnel and citizens had collected over 240,000 records in a year. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand, who said that swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel. FAO's feature of 6 May 2021 says that FAO received up to 2,500 records a day and that nearly 25 percent were unusable or incorrect. FAO asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to identify and remove the unwanted data before it shared locations with ground and air control teams. The feature says that East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. It says that they protected the food security of 36.6 million people and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses. On 15 June 2022 FAO declared the East Africa upsurge over. It said that it had trained 3,800 people across the region to use applications such as eLocust3 to report locusts. In May 2026 Serdo and Nemeth, who have no tie to FAO or PlantVillage, named eLocust3m among the tools of the 2020 to 2021 response in a review in Frontiers in Zoology. They restate FAO's figures without new analysis.

ai_role.statement: Two AI uses are documented: algorithms that double-check submitted photos (Times) and AI that filters unusable records out of FAO's daily intake (FAO). A Penn State deep-learning soil-moisture model is mentioned by the maker's university. The outcome figures belong to the entire control operation and no source isolates the AI's contribution. FAO is both co-developer and deployer, so its feature is maker-authored. The Times report is independent with named sources (Cressman, Ferrand, Hughes, Jeptoo, Owuor, Craig).

fields.account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings, and algorithms checked the photos. Penn State also extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. The wider operation also used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. On 8 April 2021 The New York Times reported that PlantVillage scouts, government personnel and citizens had collected over 240,000 records in a year. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand, who said that swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel. FAO's feature of 6 May 2021 says that FAO received up to 2,500 records a day and that nearly 25 percent were unusable or incorrect. FAO asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to identify and remove the unwanted data before it shared locations with ground and air control teams. The feature says that East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. It says that they protected the food security of 36.6 million people and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses. On 15 June 2022 FAO declared the East Africa upsurge over. It said that it had trained 3,800 people across the region to use applications such as eLocust3 to report locusts. In May 2026 Serdo and Nemeth, who have no tie to FAO or PlantVillage, named eLocust3m among the tools of the 2020 to 2021 response in a review in Frontiers in Zoology. They restate FAO's figures without new analysis.
